comments.text:
Josh Mandel, MD not my understanding.

I don't see any requirement or suggestion for you to wrap the files in a DocRef. The way I've read the spec is that you have all the files separately, concatenated together in a zip deflated .ndjson file.

"The .phr file is a single hetergenous .ndjson file that contains all of the data for a patient. It is a .ndjson file with mixed resource types. This is done to simplify the process of importing and exporting data. It is also done to simplify the process of querying data. It is easier to query a single file than it is to query multiple files. However, it does introduce import/export parsing requirements, that are not present in the Bulk Data Access format.

The generated metadata with the Composition resource and the document manifest might be different.

See also the instructions at https://build.fhir.org/ig/HL7/personal-health-record-format-ig/en/recordkeeping.html#creating-a-personal-health-record.

And https://build.fhir.org/ig/HL7/personal-health-record-format-ig/en/SphrFileType.jpg.

The benefit would be that a deterministic PHR app could then read the zip files your MyChart Takeout produces, and already know how to process the contents of the file. Thanks to the standard.

comments.text: These are sort of complementary approaches with different sets of trade-offs. FHIR API is highly structured including strong terminology support, and reasonably easy to obtain but incomplete in its coverage of the clinical record. EHI export is very well structured, But with poor terminology coverage as currently implemented, and way too difficult/ slow to obtain. The takeout approach has reasonable coverage, poor terminology support (with the possible exception of the CDAs that are included), and easy to obtain. You are absolutely right that the format or underlying apis that I use for takeout are subject to change at any time (but yes, noticing and and correcting these kinds of issues does get easier with AI)
